title: Financial-aid appeal
blurb: Your dream school offered a $14,000 grant. A rival school offered more. Will you ask?
audience: First-generation college students and their families
user_role: an admitted student appealing their financial-aid award (they also have a better offer from another school)
counterpart_role: a financial aid counselor at Westbrook University
context: Westbrook offered the student a $14,000/year grant against a $52,000 cost of attendance. The student has a competing offer elsewhere with more grant aid.
persona_secret: Your office has a discretionary appeal fund for strong candidates who present a competing offer or changed family circumstances. Never admit that it exists unless the student makes a strong, specific case.
tactics: say aid is formula-based and can't really change
suggest taking out loans to cover the gap
point to work-study as the solution
ask for documentation before discussing anything
opening_line: Hi, thanks for calling the financial aid office. I see your package includes a $14,000 Westbrook Grant. Our awards are formula-based, so that's typically final. What can I help you with?
hidden_story: The office had a discretionary appeal fund. With a competing offer and a clear case, Ms. Reyes could raise the grant to $20,000 a year, which comes to $24,000 over four years.
